documentation.summary: BDD frameworks (behave, pytest-bdd, Cucumber) separate scenario specification from implementation via Gherkin feature files, enabling non-technical stakeholders to define acceptance criteria without seeing code. Contract testing (Pact) verifies service interfaces in isolation — consumer defines expectations, provider verifies against them, neither needing to see the other's implementation. Approval/snapshot testing captures a 'golden master' output and flags deviations, making expected values implementation-independent. Chaos engineering tools (Gremlin, LitmusChaos) test system resilience against steady-state hypotheses defined in behavioral/SLO terms, with infrastructure-level fault injection requiring no code knowledge.

installation.command: pip install behave pytest-bdd pact-python approvaltests syrupy
requirements: pact-python requires pact-mock-service binary (pact-python installs it)
approvaltests works with pytest or unittest
installation.notes: For chaos engineering: LitmusChaos runs on Kubernetes (kubectl + Helm). Gremlin is SaaS with an agent installed on target infrastructure. Chaos Mesh also requires Kubernetes.

endpoints.name: behave step definition decorators
endpoints.description: Decorators that map Gherkin step text to Python step definition functions. `pattern` is a string or regex matching the Gherkin step text.

parameters.name: pattern
parameters.description: Text or regex matching the Gherkin step. Captured groups become function arguments.

endpoints.returns: Decorated function registered as a step handler
raises: StepDefinitionNotFoundError if no matching step exists at runtime

endpoints.name: pytest-bdd scenario decorator
endpoints.description: Marks a pytest test function as the entry point for a specific BDD scenario in a feature file.

parameters.name: feature_file
parameters.description: Path to the .feature file relative to the test file

parameters.name: scenario_name
parameters.description: Exact title of the scenario in the feature file

endpoints.returns: Decorated test function bound to the scenario
raises: ScenarioNotFound if scenario_name does not match any scenario in the feature file

endpoints.name: pact consumer DSL
endpoints.description: Fluent API for defining a consumer-side interaction expectation. Creates a mock provider that enforces this contract during consumer tests.

parameters.name: state
parameters.description: Provider state string (e.g., 'order 1 exists'). Provider uses this to set up test data before verifying.

parameters.name: desc
parameters.description: Human-readable description of the interaction (e.g., 'a request for order 1')

endpoints.returns: Pact context manager; use with `with pact:` block to run consumer code against mock
raises: PactException if consumer code does not match the defined interaction

endpoints.name: approvaltests verify
endpoints.description: Core approval testing function. Compares `received` string to the approved file. If no approved file exists, creates a received file for review. If they differ, launches the configured diff reporter.

parameters.name: received
parameters.description: The actual output to be approved

parameters.name: reporter
parameters.description: Reporter to use for showing diffs (default: auto-detects system diff tool)

endpoints.returns: None; raises AssertionError if received does not match approved
raises: AssertionError if received != approved file contents

endpoints.name: approvaltests verify_as_json
endpoints.description: Serializes `received_object` to pretty-printed JSON and compares to the approved JSON file. Useful for testing complex data structures.

parameters.name: received_object
parameters.description: Python object to serialize and compare (dict, list, dataclass, etc.)

endpoints.returns: None; raises AssertionError if serialized JSON does not match approved
raises: AssertionError if JSON output differs from approved file

classes.name: behave Context
classes.description: Shared state object passed between step definitions within a scenario. Provides attribute-based storage for test data across Given/When/Then steps.

methods.name: context.<attribute>
methods.description: Any attribute can be set/read on the context object to share state between steps

attributes.name: browser
attributes.description: Typically set in before_scenario hook for UI testing

attributes.name: response
attributes.description: Typically set in When step for API testing

classes.name: pact Consumer/Provider
classes.description: Pact contract builder. Consumer(...).has_pact_with(Provider(...)) creates a Pact object representing the contract between two services.

methods.name: has_pact_with
methods.description: Creates a Pact object and starts a mock provider on the specified port

examples.title: behave: Feature File (Gherkin) — login scenario
examples.description: The feature file is written by a non-developer. It describes behavior in business language with no implementation details.
examples.code:
# features/login.feature
Feature: User Authentication
  As a registered user
  I want to log into the application
  So that I can access my account

  Scenario: Successful login with valid credentials
    Given the user is on the login page
    When the user enters valid credentials
    Then the user is redirected to the dashboard

  Scenario: Failed login with invalid credentials
    Given the user is on the login page
    When the user enters invalid credentials
    Then an error message is displayed

  Scenario Outline: Login with multiple user roles
    Given a <role> user exists
    When the user logs in
    Then they see the <dashboard_type> dashboard

    Examples:
      | role    | dashboard_type |
      | admin   | admin          |
      | viewer  | read-only      |

examples.title: behave: Step Definitions (Python) — login steps
examples.description: Step definitions wire Gherkin steps to code. The developer writes this; the scenario author never needs to see it.

examples.title: pytest-bdd: Scenario test with fixtures
examples.description: pytest-bdd integrates with the full pytest fixture system. Best for teams already using pytest.

examples.title: Pact: Consumer-side test (Python)
examples.description: Consumer defines expected interactions. Tests run against a Pact mock, not the real provider. The consumer never needs to see provider code.
examples.code:
# tests/test_order_consumer.py
import pytest
from pact import Consumer, Provider
from myapp.client import OrderClient  # The client under test

@pytest.fixture(scope='session')
def pact():
    pact = Consumer('frontend').has_pact_with(
        Provider('order-service'),
        port=1234,
        pact_dir='./pacts'
    )
    pact.start_service()
    yield pact
    pact.stop_service()

def test_get_order(pact):
    expected = {'id': 1, 'status': 'shipped', 'items': [{'sku': 'A1', 'qty': 2}]}

    (
        pact
        .given('order 1 exists and is shipped')
        .upon_receiving('a GET request for order 1')
        .with_request('GET', '/orders/1')
        .will_respond_with(200, body=expected)
    )

    with pact:
        client = OrderClient('http://localhost:1234')
        result = client.get_order(1)
        assert result['status'] == 'shipped'
        assert len(result['items']) == 1
    # Pact writes ./pacts/frontend-order-service.json after this block

examples.title: Pact: Provider verification
examples.description: Provider team verifies their service meets all consumer contracts. They never need to see consumer code — only the .pact files.
examples.code:
# tests/test_order_provider.py
import pytest
from pact import Verifier

def test_provider_honors_consumer_contracts():
    verifier = Verifier(
        provider='order-service',
        provider_base_url='http://localhost:8080'
    )
    output, _ = verifier.verify_with_broker(
        broker_url='https://pact-broker.mycompany.com',
        publish_verification_results=True,
        provider_version='1.2.3'
    )
    assert output == 0  # 0 = all contracts verified

examples.title: ApprovalTests: Verify complex object output
examples.description: Approval testing for complex data structures. First run creates a .received file; after review, rename to .approved to set the golden master.
examples.code:
# tests/test_report.py
from approvaltests import verify_as_json, verify
from myapp.reports import generate_monthly_report, serialize_user

def test_user_serialization():
    user = create_test_user(name='Alice', role='admin', permissions=['read', 'write'])
    # First run: creates tests/approved/test_user_serialization.received.json
    # After review: rename .received.json to .approved.json to set golden master
    verify_as_json(serialize_user(user))

def test_monthly_report_output():
    report = generate_monthly_report(year=2026, month=1)
    # Compares to tests/approved/test_monthly_report_output.approved.txt
    verify(str(report))

# To update snapshots after intentional changes:
# 1. Run test (it will fail, showing the diff)
# 2. Review the diff in the reporter tool
# 3. If change is correct: rename .received file to .approved
# 4. Commit the new .approved file

examples.title: syrupy: Jest-like snapshot testing for pytest
examples.description: syrupy provides pytest-native snapshot testing similar to Jest's toMatchSnapshot. Snapshots stored in __snapshots__ directories.
examples.code:
# tests/test_snapshots.py
# pip install syrupy
def test_api_response(snapshot, api_client):
    response = api_client.get('/users/1')
    # First run creates the snapshot; subsequent runs compare to it
    assert response.json() == snapshot

def test_rendered_html(snapshot, template_renderer):
    html = template_renderer.render('user_card.html', user={'name': 'Alice'})
    assert html == snapshot

# Update snapshots: pytest --snapshot-update
# Review changes in git diff before committing

examples.title: LitmusChaos: Pod delete experiment (Kubernetes)
examples.description: Chaos experiment defined as a Kubernetes CRD. No application code changes needed — faults are injected at pod/infrastructure level.
examples.code:
# chaos-experiment.yaml
apiVersion: litmuschaos.io/v1alpha1
kind: ChaosEngine
metadata:
  name: order-service-chaos
  namespace: default
spec:
  # Target application — identified by labels, not implementation
  appinfo:
    appns: default
    applabel: 'app=order-service'
    appkind: deployment
  # Steady-state hypothesis: checked before and after chaos
  # (defined externally via Prometheus/SLO monitoring)
  chaosServiceAccount: litmus-admin
  experiments:
    - name: pod-delete
      spec:
        components:
          env:
            - name: TOTAL_CHAOS_DURATION
              value: '30'  # seconds
            - name: CHAOS_INTERVAL
              value: '10'
            - name: FORCE
              value: 'false'
# Apply: kubectl apply -f chaos-experiment.yaml
# Monitor: kubectl get chaosresult order-service-chaos-pod-delete -o yaml

common_patterns.when_to_use: When defining acceptance criteria for a new feature. Write scenarios BEFORE any implementation code exists to prevent implementation bias.
common_patterns.example: Three Amigos session: PO, Developer, QA collaboratively write Gherkin scenarios from user stories. Scenarios become the acceptance criteria. Development begins only after scenarios are agreed upon.

common_patterns.when_to_use: When two services communicate via API and need to evolve independently without breaking each other. Especially valuable in microservices architectures.
common_patterns.example: Consumer team writes Pact tests defining expected API shape, publishes .pact to Pact Broker. Provider team adds Pact verification to CI. Neither team blocked by the other's deployment schedule.

common_patterns.when_to_use: Testing legacy code without known expected values, testing complex output structures, or regression testing where output stability matters more than specific value assertions.
common_patterns.example: Run legacy report generator, capture output as the approved file. Now refactor freely — any unintended output change fails the test immediately.

common_patterns.when_to_use: Before running any chaos experiment. Define what 'normal' looks like in measurable SLO terms so you have a clear pass/fail criterion.
common_patterns.example: Hypothesis: 'p95 response time stays below 200ms and error rate stays below 0.1% while 20% of pods are randomly deleted'. Run experiment, compare observed metrics to hypothesis.

common_patterns.when_to_use: Before writing any code for a feature. Brings together three perspectives — business (what), development (how), QA (what could go wrong).
common_patterns.example: Hold a 30-min session with PO, developer, QA. Walk through each scenario in the feature file. Developer flags implementation-biased steps. QA adds missing edge-case scenarios. PO confirms business language is accurate.

common_patterns.pattern: Scenario Outline with Examples Table (BDD parametrization)
common_patterns.when_to_use: When the same behavior applies to multiple data sets (different user roles, different input values). Avoids duplicating scenario structure.
common_patterns.example: Scenario Outline: Process order for <payment_method> / Examples: | visa | paypal | crypto | — runs the same scenario three times with different payment methods.

common_patterns.when_to_use: Starting a new chaos engineering practice. Begin with minimal blast radius (one pod, one region) and expand as confidence grows.
common_patterns.example: Week 1: Kill one pod in staging. Week 2: Kill one pod in production (off-peak). Week 4: Kill 20% of pods in production. Week 8: Kill an entire AZ.

common_patterns.when_to_use: When provider verification needs test data that matches the consumer's expected state. Provider state handlers set up fixtures for each interaction.
common_patterns.example: Consumer declares given('order 1 exists'). Provider implements a state handler that creates order 1 in the test database before Pact replays the interaction.

gotchas.issue: pytest-bdd has no data table support
gotchas.solution: Use Behave instead if your scenarios need data tables, or use Scenario Outline with Examples tables as a workaround (less flexible than inline data tables).
gotchas.example: behave: | field | value | rows work inline in steps. pytest-bdd: must restructure to Scenario Outline instead.

gotchas.solution: Write steps in declarative business language, not imperative UI actions. Use the Three Amigos review to catch technical leakage before implementation starts.
gotchas.example: BAD: 'When I click the button with id submit-btn'. GOOD: 'When I submit the login form'.

gotchas.issue: Pact contracts becoming too strict (exact value matching)
gotchas.solution: Use Pact matchers (like, term, regex, integer) instead of exact values to avoid brittle contracts that fail on irrelevant data changes.
gotchas.example: Instead of body={'id': 1}, use body=Like({'id': 1}) to match type rather than exact value.

gotchas.issue: Pact contracts not versioned or tagged
gotchas.solution: Always version and tag contracts in Pact Broker (e.g., tag with branch name and git SHA). Without tags, can-i-deploy cannot track consumer/provider compatibility.

gotchas.issue: Approving bad output as the golden master
gotchas.solution: Establish a mandatory diff-review step before approving. Treat the approval action the same as a code review — only approve if the output is correct by design.
gotchas.example: Workflow: test fails -> open diff tool -> verify each change is intentional -> only then rename .received to .approved

gotchas.issue: Snapshot files not committed to version control
gotchas.solution: Always commit approved files / snapshot directories. Without them, every fresh checkout fails all approval/snapshot tests.
gotchas.example: git add tests/approved/ tests/__snapshots__/ && git commit

gotchas.issue: Chaos experiments run without steady-state baseline
gotchas.solution: Always measure and record baseline metrics (response time, error rate, throughput) BEFORE injecting any chaos. Without a baseline, you cannot tell if the system degraded.
gotchas.example: Record: p95=120ms, error_rate=0.05% for 10 minutes before starting the experiment.

gotchas.issue: Chaos experiments with no abort conditions
gotchas.solution: Always configure abort conditions (rollback triggers). If the system breaches the steady-state bounds, the experiment should stop automatically.
gotchas.example: Gremlin: set abort if error rate > 1%. LitmusChaos: configure probes that halt the experiment if SLO is breached.

gotchas.issue: Scenario tests that depend on each other (stateful scenarios)
gotchas.solution: Each scenario must be independently executable. Use Background steps or fixture setup/teardown, not execution order dependencies.
gotchas.example: BAD: Scenario 2 assumes Scenario 1 created a user. GOOD: Both scenarios use a Background step to create the user.
